source_refs.note: Book p. 191: 10.4 Double Angle Identities, recall of sum formulas, derivations (i) sin 2a, (ii) cos 2a three forms, (iii) tan 2a; starts below Exercise 10.2 Q15 on the same page

blocks.text:
We have discussed the following results:
\[\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta\]
\[\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta\]
\[\tan(\alpha + \beta) = \dfrac{\tan\alpha + \tan\beta}{1 - \tan\alpha\tan\beta}\]
We can use them to obtain the double angle identities as follows:

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: A double angle is twice an angle: \(2\alpha\). Since \(2\alpha = \alpha + \alpha\), we only have to put \(\beta = \alpha\) in the sum formulas. No new idea is needed; the double angle identities are special cases of the results of 10.1.2.

(i) Put \(\beta = \alpha\) in \(\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta\):
\[\sin(\alpha + \alpha) = \sin\alpha\cos\alpha + \cos\alpha\sin\alpha\]
The two terms on the right are equal, so they add up to twice one of them. Hence

blocks.text_alt: sin 2 alpha equals 2 sin alpha cos alpha

blocks.text:
(ii) Put \(\beta = \alpha\) in \(\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta\):
\[\cos(\alpha + \alpha) = \cos\alpha\cos\alpha - \sin\alpha\sin\alpha\]
\[\cos 2\alpha = \cos^{2}\alpha - \sin^{2}\alpha\]
Using \(\sin^{2}\alpha = 1 - \cos^{2}\alpha\):
\[\cos 2\alpha = \cos^{2}\alpha - (1 - \cos^{2}\alpha)\]
\[= \cos^{2}\alpha - 1 + \cos^{2}\alpha\]
\[\cos 2\alpha = 2\cos^{2}\alpha - 1\]
Again from \(\cos 2\alpha = \cos^{2}\alpha - \sin^{2}\alpha\), using \(\cos^{2}\alpha = 1 - \sin^{2}\alpha\):
\[\cos 2\alpha = (1 - \sin^{2}\alpha) - \sin^{2}\alpha\]
\[\cos 2\alpha = 1 - 2\sin^{2}\alpha\]

blocks.text_alt: cos 2 alpha equals cos squared alpha minus sin squared alpha
cos 2 alpha equals 2 cos squared alpha minus 1
cos 2 alpha equals 1 minus 2 sin squared alpha

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Which form should you use? Choose the one that contains what is given or what you need:
only \(\cos\alpha\) known: use \(2\cos^{2}\alpha - 1\); only \(\sin\alpha\) known: use \(1 - 2\sin^{2}\alpha\); both known: \(\cos^{2}\alpha - \sin^{2}\alpha\).
Rearranging the last two forms gives two very useful results:
\[1 + \cos 2\alpha = 2\cos^{2}\alpha\]
\[1 - \cos 2\alpha = 2\sin^{2}\alpha\]
They turn a square into a first power of cosine. They are the starting point of the half angle identities in 10.5.

blocks.text_alt: tan 2 alpha equals 2 tan alpha over 1 minus tan squared alpha

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The tangent formula works only when \(\tan\alpha\) exists and \(\tan^{2}\alpha \ne 1\). For example, for \(\alpha = 45^{\circ}\) the denominator is \(1 - 1 = 0\): indeed \(\tan 90^{\circ}\) is undefined.

blocks.title: Exam tip
Key points
blocks.text:
1. Double angle identities come from the sum formulas with \(\beta = \alpha\).
2. \(\sin 2\alpha = 2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha\).
3. \(\cos 2\alpha = \cos^{2}\alpha - \sin^{2}\alpha = 2\cos^{2}\alpha - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^{2}\alpha\).
4. \(\tan 2\alpha = \frac{2\tan\alpha}{1 - \tan^{2}\alpha}\), provided \(\tan^{2}\alpha \ne 1\).
5. \(1 + \cos 2\alpha = 2\cos^{2}\alpha\) and \(1 - \cos 2\alpha = 2\sin^{2}\alpha\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(\sin 2\alpha = 2\sin\alpha\). The 2 is inside the angle; \(\sin 60^{\circ} \ne 2\sin 30^{\circ}\) (\(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \ne 1\)).
2. Mixing up the forms: it is \(2\cos^{2}\alpha - 1\) but \(1 - 2\sin^{2}\alpha\) (the 1 changes side).
3. Writing \(1 + \tan^{2}\alpha\) in the denominator of \(\tan 2\alpha\); it is \(1 - \tan^{2}\alpha\).
